n: Daniel’s final vision (chapters 10–12) comes in the third year of Cyrus, about 536 BC. By now some Jews had returned to Jerusalem, but Daniel, now very old, remained in Persia. The message was true but concerned a long, hard conflict.

f.w: the third year of Cyrus king of Persia

f.g: Or “it concerned a great conflict (or hardship).”

n: Daniel had been mourning for three full weeks—perhaps grieving over troubles facing the returned exiles, whose temple rebuilding met opposition.
He fasted partially—no rich food, meat, or wine—and did not use the scented oils normally applied to the skin. His fast showed earnest seeking.

f.g: Using olive oil on the skin was a daily comfort; skipping it was a sign of mourning.

n: On the 24th day of the first month—just after Passover—Daniel is by the Tigris River.
He sees a man in linen with a belt of fine gold. Linen was worn by priests and heavenly messengers.

f.g: A place known for fine gold; location uncertain.

n: His body gleams like a gemstone, his face like lightning, his eyes like flaming torches, his limbs like polished bronze, and his voice like a roaring crowd. John’s vision of the resurrected Christ in Revelation is strikingly similar.

f.g: A precious stone, possibly yellow chrysolite or topaz.

f.w: his eyes as lamps of fire

n: Only Daniel sees the vision. His companions feel terror and run to hide—like Paul’s companions on the road to Damascus.

f.w: the men that were with me saw not the vision

n: Left alone, Daniel loses all strength; his healthy color drains away. Encountering heavenly glory is physically overwhelming for mortals.

f.w: my comeliness was turned in me into corruption
f.g: My healthy appearance turned deathly pale.

f.w: there remained no strength in me

n: At the sound of the voice, Daniel falls face-down into a deep stupor.

f.w: in a deep sleep on my face

n: A hand touches him and lifts him, trembling, onto his hands and knees.
The messenger calls him “greatly beloved,” tells him to stand, and explains that he has been sent to him. Daniel stands, trembling.
“Fear not.” From the very first day Daniel humbled himself to seek understanding, his prayer was heard. The messenger came because of his prayer.

f.g: Prayer is heard at once, even if the answer is delayed.
To humble yourself, as by fasting.

n: The delay had a cause: a spiritual opponent, “the prince of the kingdom of Persia,” resisted for 21 days—the same length as Daniel’s fast—until Michael came to help. This verse lifts the curtain on unseen spiritual conflict behind earthly events.

f.w: the prince of the kingdom of Persia
f.g: A spiritual power influencing Persia—not the human king.

f.w: Michael, one of the chief princes
f.g: Latter-day Saint scripture identifies Michael the archangel as Adam.

n: The messenger has come to explain what will happen to Daniel’s people in the latter days—a vision reaching far into the future.
Overcome again, Daniel bows his face to the ground and can’t speak.
Someone in human likeness touches his lips, and he can speak again. He explains that the vision has filled him with anguish and drained his strength.

f.w: my sorrows are turned upon me
f.g: Pangs of distress, like labor pains, have gripped me.

n: “How can someone like me talk with someone like you?” He has no strength and can barely breathe.
Again the human-like figure touches him and gives him strength.
“Don’t be afraid, greatly beloved. Peace. Be strong—be strong!” As the words are spoken, strength comes. God’s word itself empowers.

f.w: peace be unto thee, be strong

n: The messenger must return to fight the prince of Persia, and afterward the prince of Greece will come—another empire with its own spiritual powers behind it.

f.g: The spiritual power behind Greece, the kingdom to follow Persia.

n: He will reveal what is written in “the book of truth”—God’s record of the future. Only Michael, Israel’s guardian prince, stands with him in this conflict.

f.g: God’s book of decrees—His record of what will happen.
